title: The hidden costs of operational friction
summary: Poor handoffs between teams increase costs and frustrate customers. Learn where operational friction occurs and how leaders can address it.
body_markdown:
### Every team can do its job well, and the company can still fail the customer.


I almost walked away from a rental car company because of one frustrating experience.


I was standing at the rental counter, trying to resolve an issue, when the employee told me, "You’ll need to call customer service. I can’t fix that here." So I called. Right there, in front of him.


I was transferred four times, and each time I had to explain everything again: my name, my reservation, what had happened. Meanwhile, the employee sat across from me, watching me get transferred over and over. I couldn’t believe I had to call a company I was standing inside just to get help.


Everyone I spoke with was polite and trying to help, but because my data didn’t travel with me, my experience was terrible. The episode encapsulates a problem I see in organizations of every size: operational friction. It’s something that doesn’t show up on a dashboard, but quietly drives up costs and wears down patience and loyalty.


**Customers don’t experience the org chart. They experience the company.**


**The blind spots**


Companies spend millions improving how individual departments work. On paper, everything can look great. One team meets its service levels. Another processes work faster. The contact center answers calls on time. But the customer is still waiting.


How does that happen? Because some of the biggest problems aren’t happening inside individual departments. They’re happening between them.


Every time work moves from one team to another, there’s a chance something gets missed or delayed. A form gets submitted but doesn’t reach the right team. A decision made in one system doesn’t show up in another. A customer moves from chat to phone and becomes a stranger again.


Each team is accountable for its own work, but what happens between steps belongs to no one.


**The everyday costs**


These gaps don’t usually show up as a separate expense on a financial report — yet they cost companies every day.


- **Repeat calls.** Every time a customer has to call back to re-explain the same issue, you’re paying for a problem that should have been resolved.
- **Rework.** Employees spend time looking for missing documents or re-entering information that was already captured somewhere else.
- **Delays.** Work sits in queues waiting for another team to pick it up. Every handoff adds more time.
- **Lost customers.** People don’t remember which department caused the problem. They remember the experience, and they remember the company.
- **Frustrated employees.** Your people feel it too. No one enjoys apologizing for something they have no control over.


Businesses can invest heavily in improving productivity and still lose the savings to poor handoffs. In my rental car experience, the company paid multiple employees to handle the same issue, and I became more frustrated with every transfer. A process isn’t efficient if it takes that many people to solve one problem.


**Where leaders and teams should look**


Improving a department doesn’t always improve the customer experience. To find the friction, leaders and teams need to look at how work moves between departments.


Key questions to ask and answer:


- **Where does work get stuck?** Map customer and interdepartmental journeys and look closely at what happens at every handoff.
- **Why are we doing the same work twice?** Find where information gets entered again or customers have to repeat themselves.
- **Who owns the final outcome?** If everyone is responsible, there’s a good chance nobody really owns it.
- **Are we measuring the right things?** It’s not enough to know how quickly each team finishes its part. What matters is how long it takes to solve the customer’s problem.


This isn’t about blaming people. The employee at the rental counter was doing what his process allowed him to do. The people answering the phones were doing their jobs too. The problem was that nobody seemed equipped to help me from start to finish. That’s what leaders need to fix, and that’s where opportunity lies.


**Closing the gaps**


During our recent webinar, *[The experience is only as good as the work behind it](https://insights.conduent.com/youtube-all-videos/the-experience-is-only-as-good-as-the-work-behind-it)* , my colleague Mandy Huckaby made a point that stayed with me: “Every element that we improve behind the scenes makes for an even better conversation in front of it.”


In healthcare, missing information can send a claim back through the process, creating more work and delaying an answer. AI and[automation in healthcare operations](https://insights.conduent.com/conduent-blog/admin-overload-healthcare-automation?_gl=1*185uwz3*_up*MQ..*_ga*ODM3NjMzMjA1LjE3OTMzMDQ5OTE.*_ga_TPCLJS6Y05*czE3OTMzMDQ5OTAkbzEkZzEkdDE3OTMzMDY2NzckajYwJGwwJGgw) can help catch those gaps early, reducing rework and lowering costs.


**Making one step faster doesn’t help much if the work gets stuck at the next one.**


At Conduent, we see the same challenges in banking and other industries through our work with clients around the globe. That work has sharpened our view into where information, decisions and work become disconnected — and how much time and money gets wasted when work doesn’t move smoothly between teams.


Connecting the work matters just as much as automating it. When we get both right, we can reduce costs and make things easier for customers.


**Every team can do its job well, and the company can still fail the customer.**


So the next time you review your operations, look past the boxes on the org chart. Don’t just ask how well each team is performing — ask how well they’re working together.
